flashcards.front: Name the six elements of the communication process.
flashcards.back: Sender, message, encoding, channel, decoding, receiver (+ feedback and noise).

flashcards.front: What is 'noise' in the communication process?
flashcards.back: Any interference — physical (loud room), semantic (jargon), or psychological (bias) — that distorts the message.

flashcards.front: What is non-verbal communication?
flashcards.back: Messages conveyed without words — body language, facial expressions, gestures, eye contact, and proxemics (personal space).

flashcards.front: What is feedback in communication?
flashcards.back: The receiver's response that tells the sender whether the message was understood correctly.

quizItems.prompt: In the communication process, the CHANNEL refers to:
options: The medium through which the message is transmitted
The person who receives the message
The noise that distorts the message
quizItems.answer: The medium through which the message is transmitted
quizItems.explanation: The channel is the means of transmission — e.g. email, face-to-face conversation, phone call.

quizItems.prompt: Using technical jargon that the audience does not understand creates which type of noise?
quizItems.answer: Semantic noise
quizItems.explanation: Semantic noise arises from words or symbols that carry different meanings for sender and receiver.

quizItems.prompt: Which component confirms that the message was correctly received and understood?
quizItems.answer: Feedback
quizItems.explanation: Feedback closes the communication loop by confirming receipt and comprehension of the message.

workedExamples.title: Identifying Noise in a Lecture
workedExamples.summary: Apply the communication model to a classroom scenario.
workedExamples.problem: A lecturer explains a complex accounting concept to 80 students. Some students are chatting; others do not understand the terminology used. Identify the communication elements and any noise present.

steps.label: Identify elements
steps.explanation: Sender = lecturer; Message = accounting concept; Channel = verbal/visual (lecture + slides); Receivers = students.

steps.label: Identify noise — physical
steps.explanation: Students chatting creates physical noise that disrupts reception of the message.

steps.label: Identify noise — semantic
steps.explanation: Complex terminology creates semantic noise — students don't know the jargon.

steps.label: Suggest improvement
steps.explanation: Lecturer should simplify language, ask for feedback (e.g. 'any questions?') and manage classroom noise.

workedExamples.answer: Physical noise (chatting) and semantic noise (jargon) are present; feedback is needed to confirm understanding.

flashcards.front: What does SQ3R stand for?
flashcards.back: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review — a structured approach to active reading.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between skimming and scanning?
flashcards.back: Skimming = reading quickly for an overview of the whole text. Scanning = searching for a specific piece of information.

flashcards.front: What is the 'Survey' step in SQ3R?
flashcards.back: Skim the text first — read headings, subheadings, first sentences of paragraphs and summaries to get an overview before reading in full.

flashcards.front: What is an inference in academic reading?
flashcards.back: A conclusion drawn from evidence in the text that is not directly stated — reading between the lines.

quizItems.prompt: In SQ3R, the 'Question' step involves:
options: Turning headings into questions before reading
Writing a summary of the text
quizItems.answer: Turning headings into questions before reading
quizItems.explanation: The Question step converts headings/subheadings into questions to create a reading purpose and improve focus.

quizItems.prompt: You need to find the date of a specific event in a history article. You should use:
quizItems.answer: Scanning
quizItems.explanation: Scanning means searching quickly for a specific keyword or fact without reading the whole text.

quizItems.prompt: The final step of SQ3R is 'Review', which means:
options: Rereading the text from the beginning
Going back over notes and testing recall of key ideas
Writing a new question for each paragraph
quizItems.answer: Going back over notes and testing recall of key ideas
quizItems.explanation: Review consolidates learning by returning to notes, recalling answers to the questions generated earlier, and identifying gaps.

workedExamples.title: Applying SQ3R to a Textbook Chapter
workedExamples.summary: Walk through the SQ3R method on a business textbook chapter.
workedExamples.problem: You must read Chapter 3 of your Business Management textbook ('Forms of Business Ownership') before tomorrow's lecture. Apply SQ3R.

steps.label: S — Survey
steps.explanation: Read the chapter title, all headings (sole trader, partnership, company), the chapter summary, and any bold terms. Takes 3 minutes.

steps.label: Q — Question
steps.explanation: Convert headings to questions: 'What is a sole trader?' 'What are the advantages of a partnership?' Write these in your notes.

steps.label: R — Read
steps.explanation: Read each section actively, looking for the answers to your questions. Highlight or underline key definitions.

steps.label: R — Recite
steps.explanation: After each section, close the book and recite the answer to your question from memory.

steps.label: R — Review
steps.explanation: After finishing the chapter, review all your answers and any sections where you couldn't recite correctly.

workedExamples.answer: SQ3R turns passive reading into active learning: Survey → Question → Read → Recite → Review.

flashcards.front: Describe the three sections of the Cornell note-taking page.
flashcards.back: Right column (notes area, 6cm wide): main content. Left column (cue/question area, 3cm): keywords and questions. Bottom strip (summary, 5cm): brief summary of the page.

flashcards.front: What is the advantage of a mind map over linear notes?
flashcards.back: Mind maps show relationships between ideas visually, use both hemispheres of the brain and are easier to review at a glance.

flashcards.front: What should go in the 'cue column' of Cornell notes?
flashcards.back: Key terms, questions, and headings that test your recall of the main notes column — used for active self-testing.

flashcards.front: When should you complete Cornell notes after a lecture?
flashcards.back: Within 24 hours — research shows memory decay is fastest in the first day after learning.

quizItems.prompt: In the Cornell system, what belongs in the bottom summary strip?
options: A brief 2-4 sentence summary of the page's main idea
A list of all vocabulary terms
quizItems.answer: A brief 2-4 sentence summary of the page's main idea
quizItems.explanation: The summary section forces synthesis of the page into a brief overview, aiding long-term retention.

quizItems.prompt: A mind map is MOST useful for:
options: Organising brainstormed ideas and showing relationships
Recording exact quotations from a textbook
quizItems.answer: Organising brainstormed ideas and showing relationships
quizItems.explanation: Mind maps excel at visually organising concepts and revealing how ideas connect — ideal for brainstorming and revision.

quizItems.prompt: The cue column in Cornell notes is used to:
options: Write keywords and self-test questions after the lecture
quizItems.answer: Write keywords and self-test questions after the lecture
quizItems.explanation: The cue column is completed after the lecture and used to test recall by covering the notes column.

workedExamples.title: Creating Cornell Notes from a Lecture
workedExamples.summary: Convert raw lecture notes into a Cornell format.
workedExamples.problem: After a lecture on 'Forms of Business Ownership', your raw notes include: 'Sole trader — 1 owner, unlimited liability, easy to start.' Convert this to Cornell format.

steps.label: Step 1 — Notes column
steps.explanation: Right column: 'Sole trader: owned by 1 person. Advantages: easy to set up, full control. Disadvantage: UNLIMITED LIABILITY — personal assets at risk.'

steps.label: Step 2 — Cue column
steps.explanation: Left column: 'Q: What is the main risk of sole trader?' and keyword: 'unlimited liability'.

steps.label: Step 3 — Summary
steps.explanation: Bottom strip: 'A sole trader is a simple one-person business that is easy to start but exposes the owner to unlimited personal liability.'

workedExamples.answer: Cornell format separates main content (right), keywords/questions (left), and summary (bottom) for effective review.

flashcards.front: What are the three main parts of an oral presentation?
flashcards.back: Introduction (attention-getter, purpose, preview), Body (2-4 main points with support), Conclusion (summary, memorable close).

flashcards.front: Name three techniques to reduce presentation anxiety.
flashcards.back: Preparation and practice; controlled breathing; reframing anxiety as excitement; positive visualisation.

flashcards.front: What is the 6x6 rule for PowerPoint slides?
flashcards.back: No more than 6 bullet points per slide and no more than 6 words per bullet — keeps slides clean and focused.

flashcards.front: What is eye contact's role in a presentation?
flashcards.back: Builds credibility and connection with the audience; demonstrates confidence and helps hold attention.

quizItems.prompt: What is the PRIMARY purpose of the introduction in an oral presentation?
options: To present all the supporting evidence
To grab attention, state the purpose and preview the structure
quizItems.answer: To grab attention, state the purpose and preview the structure
quizItems.explanation: A strong introduction orients the audience: why should they listen, what will they learn, and how is the presentation structured.

quizItems.prompt: Reading directly from your notes during a presentation is problematic because it:
options: Reduces eye contact and audience engagement
quizItems.answer: Reduces eye contact and audience engagement
quizItems.explanation: Eye contact and natural delivery are key to audience engagement; reading from notes breaks this connection.

quizItems.prompt: The 6x6 rule in slide design recommends:
options: 6 slides per presentation and 6 minutes per slide
No more than 6 bullet points and 6 words per bullet per slide
Six colours and six fonts per presentation
quizItems.answer: No more than 6 bullet points and 6 words per bullet per slide
quizItems.explanation: The 6x6 rule prevents overcrowded slides and encourages the presenter to speak to points rather than read from the screen.

workedExamples.title: Structuring a 5-Minute Presentation
workedExamples.summary: Plan the structure of a short academic presentation.
workedExamples.problem: You must deliver a 5-minute presentation on 'The Importance of Entrepreneurship in SA'. Plan the introduction, body and conclusion.

steps.label: Introduction (1 min)
steps.explanation: Attention-getter: 'South Africa has a 32% unemployment rate. Entrepreneurs create the jobs we need.' State purpose: 'Today I'll argue that entrepreneurship is SA's best tool against unemployment.' Preview: 'I'll cover 3 reasons.'

steps.label: Body (3 min)
steps.explanation: Point 1: Job creation — cite NBS stats on SMME employment. Point 2: Innovation — SA tech startups (e.g. Yoco, PayFast). Point 3: Economic empowerment — B-BBEE and township entrepreneurship.

steps.label: Conclusion (1 min)
steps.explanation: Summarise three points. Memorable close: 'Every great SA business started with one person who decided to begin.'

workedExamples.answer: Structure: Introduction (1 min) + Body with 3 points (3 min) + Conclusion (1 min) = 5 minutes.

flashcards.front: List the five components of a professional email.
flashcards.back: Subject line, salutation, body (opening/middle/close), sign-off, and signature.

flashcards.front: What is the 'you-attitude' in professional writing?
flashcards.back: Focusing on the reader's needs and benefits rather than the writer's perspective — use 'you' more than 'I'.

flashcards.front: What is an appropriate salutation in a formal email to a lecturer?
flashcards.back: 'Dear Prof. Smith,' or 'Dear Dr. Nkosi,' — use title and surname, not first name or 'Hey'.

flashcards.front: What makes a subject line effective in a professional email?
flashcards.back: It is specific, concise and informative — e.g. 'BMAN111 Assignment Query — Student 12345678' not just 'Hi' or 'Question'.

quizItems.prompt: Which subject line is MOST appropriate for a formal email to your lecturer?
quizItems.answer: BMAN111 — Assignment 2 Submission Query — 34567890
quizItems.explanation: An effective subject line is specific and informative, allowing the recipient to immediately understand the email's purpose.

quizItems.prompt: The you-attitude in 'You will benefit from attending this workshop' is better than:
options: I think the workshop is good
The workshop will occur on Friday
quizItems.answer: I think the workshop is good
quizItems.explanation: The you-attitude focuses on the reader's benefit ('you will benefit') rather than the writer's perspective ('I think').

quizItems.prompt: In a formal email, the sign-off 'Cheers,' is:
options: Too informal for a professional or academic email
quizItems.answer: Too informal for a professional or academic email
quizItems.explanation: Formal sign-offs include 'Kind regards', 'Yours sincerely', or 'Regards'. 'Cheers' is informal and inappropriate in academic/professional contexts.

workedExamples.title: Rewriting an Informal Email as a Professional Email
workedExamples.summary: Transform a poorly written student email into a professional one.
workedExamples.problem: Original email: 'Hey prof!! i missed the test bc i was sick. when can i write?? thx'. Rewrite professionally.

steps.label: Subject line
steps.explanation: ICOM111 — Missed Class Test — Request for Alternative Assessment — Student 34567890

steps.label: Salutation
steps.explanation: Dear Prof. Van der Merwe,

steps.label: Body — opening
steps.explanation: I am a student in your ICOM111 Tuesday morning class (student number 34567890).

steps.label: Body — middle
steps.explanation: I regret to inform you that I was unable to attend the class test on [date] due to illness. I have attached a medical certificate for your records.

steps.label: Body — close
steps.explanation: I would be grateful if you could advise me on the procedure for requesting an alternative assessment opportunity.

steps.label: Sign-off
steps.explanation: Kind regards, [Full Name], Student No. 34567890

workedExamples.answer: A professional email uses formal salutation, clear purpose, you-attitude, polite close, and appropriate sign-off.

flashcards.front: List the main sections of a formal report in order.
flashcards.back: Cover page → Table of contents → Executive summary → Introduction → Body (findings) → Conclusions → Recommendations → References → Appendices.

flashcards.front: What is an executive summary and who reads it?
flashcards.back: A 1-page overview of the report's purpose, key findings and recommendations — written for busy executives and decision-makers who may not read the full report.

flashcards.front: What is a memo report?
flashcards.back: An internal informal report formatted as a memo (To/From/Date/Subject), used for routine internal business communication.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between findings and conclusions in a report?
flashcards.back: Findings are the factual results/data gathered. Conclusions are interpretations drawn from the findings. Recommendations follow from conclusions.

quizItems.prompt: The executive summary of a report should be written:
options: After the full report is complete
As the first step in report planning
By someone other than the report author
quizItems.answer: After the full report is complete
quizItems.explanation: The executive summary summarises the completed report — it cannot be written until all findings and conclusions are known.

quizItems.prompt: Which section of a report presents the factual data gathered during research?
quizItems.answer: Findings
quizItems.explanation: The findings section presents factual, objective results from research or investigation without interpretation.

quizItems.prompt: A memo report is BEST suited for:
options: A report submitted to external clients
quizItems.answer: Internal communication within an organisation
quizItems.explanation: Memo reports use the informal To/From/Date/Subject format and are intended for internal audiences only.

workedExamples.title: Writing an Executive Summary
workedExamples.summary: Draft an executive summary from a given set of report facts.
workedExamples.problem: A report investigated absenteeism at a call centre. Findings: absenteeism is 18% (target: 5%); main causes are low morale (45%) and long commutes (30%). Recommendation: introduce a hybrid working policy. Write an executive summary (max 100 words).

steps.label: Opening sentence — purpose
steps.explanation: State what the report investigated.

steps.label: Key finding
steps.explanation: Absenteeism is 18%, significantly above the 5% target.

steps.label: Main causes
steps.explanation: The primary drivers are low employee morale (45% of cases) and long commute times (30%).

steps.label: Recommendation
steps.explanation: It is recommended that a hybrid working policy be introduced to reduce commute burden and improve morale.

workedExamples.answer: Executive summary: This report investigated absenteeism at [Call Centre]. Absenteeism stands at 18%, well above the 5% target. Analysis identifies low morale (45%) and long commutes (30%) as primary drivers. It is recommended that a hybrid working policy be implemented to address both factors.

flashcards.front: What is a meeting agenda?
flashcards.back: A written list of items to be discussed at a meeting, circulated to participants in advance so they can prepare.

flashcards.front: What are minutes of a meeting?
flashcards.back: The official written record of what was discussed, decided and action items assigned at a meeting.

flashcards.front: What is the role of the chairperson in a meeting?
flashcards.back: Facilitates the meeting, keeps it on agenda and on time, manages participation, and ensures decisions are made.

flashcards.front: Name two causes of conflict in groups.
flashcards.back: Differing goals or values; unclear roles or responsibilities; poor communication; competition for resources.

quizItems.prompt: Who is responsible for taking minutes during a meeting?
quizItems.answer: The secretary
quizItems.explanation: The secretary is the designated note-taker who records proceedings and produces the official minutes.

quizItems.prompt: What should meeting minutes include?
options: Attendance, decisions made, and action items with owners and deadlines
Only the final decisions, not the discussion
The full script of everything said
quizItems.answer: Attendance, decisions made, and action items with owners and deadlines
quizItems.explanation: Minutes record who was present, what was decided, and who is responsible for each action by when.

quizItems.prompt: The first item on most formal meeting agendas is:
quizItems.answer: Confirmation of previous minutes
quizItems.explanation: Confirming the previous meeting's minutes ensures accuracy of the official record before proceeding with new business.

workedExamples.title: Drafting a Meeting Agenda
workedExamples.summary: Create a structured agenda for a student group project meeting.
workedExamples.problem: Your BMAN111 group needs to meet to finalise your group assignment. Draft an agenda for a 45-minute meeting.

steps.label: Heading
steps.explanation: BMAN111 Group Assignment Meeting | Date: 10 April 2026 | Time: 14:00 | Venue: Library Study Room 3 | Attendees: Sipho, Lerato, James, Fatima

steps.label: Item 1 — Welcome and apologies (5 min)
steps.explanation: Chairperson opens the meeting; note any apologies.

steps.label: Item 2 — Confirm previous actions (5 min)
steps.explanation: Review tasks assigned at last meeting; confirm completion.

steps.label: Item 3 — Review draft sections (20 min)
steps.explanation: Each member presents their completed section; group provides feedback.

steps.label: Item 4 — Final formatting and submission (10 min)
steps.explanation: Agree on formatting, assign final edit to one person, confirm submission date.

steps.label: Item 5 — AOB and close (5 min)
steps.explanation: Any other business; chairperson closes meeting.

workedExamples.answer: A structured 45-minute agenda: Welcome → Confirm actions → Review sections → Finalise submission → AOB.
